client: Hey Luna, I've been really struggling lately with this one thing. Every time I have to go to the café where my ex and I used to meet, my heart starts racing and I feel completely overwhelmed. I know it's been a while since we broke up, but it just doesn't seem to get any easier. I'm not sure if therapy can even help with this, to be honest.
therapist: Hi there, I can really understand how challenging and overwhelming those moments must be for you. It’s completely normal to still feel this way, even after some time has passed. Can you tell me more about what goes through your mind when you’re in that café, or what specific thoughts or memories come up?

client: When I'm in the café, I often feel like everyone is judging me, and I start to think about all the times I've felt embarrassed or awkward in social situations. It’s like I’m replaying all these moments in my head, and it just makes me want to leave. It’s hard to shake off those thoughts, even when I know they’re not realistic.
therapist: It sounds like those thoughts and memories can really weigh on you and make you feel very self-conscious. It’s understandable that you’d want to leave to escape those feelings. Have you noticed any specific triggers in the café that seem to bring these thoughts to the surface, or are there any particular moments when they become more intense?

client: Yeah, it’s definitely the quiet moments that get to me the most. When it’s busy, I can distract myself, but when it’s quiet, I start overthinking and feel like everyone is watching me. It’s hard because I can’t always predict when those moments will happen.
therapist: It makes sense that the quiet moments would be tougher, especially when you feel more exposed and self-conscious. It’s natural to try to distract yourself when it’s busy, but those quieter times can bring up a lot of thoughts and feelings. Have you tried any strategies to manage those moments, like focusing on your breathing or bringing a book to read?

client: I've tried breathing exercises before, but they don't always help. It's hard because the quiet moments feel so heavy, and sometimes I just feel like I'm drowning in my own thoughts. Bringing a book sounds like a good idea, but I worry that I won't be able to concentrate and it might just make me feel more frustrated.
therapist: It sounds like those quiet moments can be really intense and overwhelming, and it’s completely understandable that you might feel like you’re drowning in your thoughts. Breathing exercises can be helpful, but they don’t always work for everyone or in every situation. Bringing a book is a good idea, and if you find it hard to concentrate, maybe you could also try something simpler, like focusing on the sensations around you—like the sounds or the feel of the chair. What do you think about trying a different distraction technique, or maybe even just acknowledging your thoughts without trying to push them away?

client: I appreciate the suggestions, but it's hard because those thoughts are so persistent. I feel like they follow me everywhere, and sometimes even trying to acknowledge them just makes them louder. I’m not sure if a different distraction technique will work any better.
therapist: I can see how exhausting and persistent those thoughts can be, and it’s completely understandable that they feel like they’re following you everywhere. It’s tough when acknowledging them doesn’t seem to help and just makes them louder. Have you ever tried journaling about these thoughts or talking them through with someone you trust? Sometimes getting them out in a different way can provide some relief or new insights.

client: I've tried journaling a few times, but it feels like I'm just writing the same things over and over. It doesn't really help me feel any better. Talking to someone I trust sounds good in theory, but I worry they won't understand or will just tell me what I already know. It's hard to open up when you feel so alone.
therapist: It sounds like you’ve been trying different strategies, but they haven’t provided the relief you’re looking for, and that can be really frustrating. It’s understandable to feel alone and worried about opening up to someone, especially if you’re concerned they might not fully understand or offer the same advice you’ve already heard. What do you think might help you feel more comfortable or supported when sharing your feelings with someone?

client: I really appreciate that you understand how frustrating it can be. I guess what makes it hard is that I often feel like people just don’t get it, and I end up feeling more alone. Maybe if I could find someone who really listens and doesn’t just give the same old advice, it would help, but I’m not sure how to make that happen.
therapist: I completely understand how isolating it can feel when it seems like others don’t truly get what you’re going through. It’s important to have someone who listens without just giving the same old advice. Have you considered reaching out to a support group or a therapist who specializes in these kinds of issues? Sometimes, finding someone who has a deeper understanding can make a big difference. What do you think about exploring that option, or is there another way you might feel more comfortable connecting with someone who can really listen?

client: I appreciate the suggestion, but I'm not sure a support group or another therapist would really change things. I've tried talking to people before, and it just feels like they end up giving the same advice or don't really get it. It's hard for me to open up and trust that someone will truly understand.
therapist: I can totally understand your hesitation and the frustration you feel when it seems like others don’t truly get it. It’s really hard to open up and trust that someone will truly understand, especially when you’ve had those experiences before. What do you think might help you feel more confident in opening up to someone, or are there specific qualities you’re looking for in a supportive person?

client: I appreciate that you get how hard it is to open up. I guess I just need someone who really listens and doesn’t judge. It’s hard because I’ve been let down before, and I worry that even if I do find someone, they might not really understand or stick around.
therapist: I completely understand how important it is to find someone who listens without judgment and really gets what you’re going through. It’s completely valid to be cautious after being let down before. Building trust takes time, and it’s okay to take things at your own pace. What are some qualities or actions that you think would help you feel more comfortable and supported when opening up to someone?

client: I appreciate that you understand my concerns. For me, feeling comfortable and supported means knowing that the person genuinely cares and won’t dismiss my feelings. It’s also important that they can handle the intensity of my emotions without getting overwhelmed or shutting down. It’s hard to open up when I feel like I might be too much for someone to handle.
therapist: I really appreciate you sharing that with me. It’s so important to feel like the person you’re talking to genuinely cares and can handle the intensity of your emotions without getting overwhelmed. It’s completely understandable that you want to feel safe and supported. What do you think might help you feel more confident in finding someone who can provide that kind of support, or are there any small steps you could take to start building that kind of connection?
